headline: Simple Vitamin C Supplement Shows Promise for Blood Cancer Prevention
meta_description: A clinical trial reveals that daily vitamin C supplementation may improve survival in patients with precancerous blood disorders, offering hope for cancer inte…
summary_short: A landmark study finds that taking 1,000 mg of vitamin C daily could help people with precancerous blood conditions live longer and experience fewer complications.
body:
In a first-of-its-kind randomized trial, scientists have discovered that a simple, inexpensive intervention may help protect people from leukemia. The EVITA clinical trial, conducted by researchers at Van Andel Institute and led by Dr. Kirsten Grønbæk at the University of Copenhagen, found that patients with precancerous blood disorders who took 1,000 mg of oral vitamin C daily for one year experienced fewer adverse events and showed a significant survival advantage after three years of follow-up compared to those receiving a placebo. The findings, published in the American Cancer Society journal CANCER, represent the first rigorous test of oral vitamin C supplementation in patients at risk of developing blood cancers—a departure from earlier studies that focused on intravenous vitamin C and solid tumors.

The 109-patient trial enrolled people with conditions like clonal cytopenia of undetermined significance (CCUS) and myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), both of which can progress to acute myeloid leukemia. Currently, no approved treatment can prevent these precancerous conditions from becoming leukemia. Many older adults with MDS cannot undergo stem cell transplantation, the available treatment option, due to age or other medical factors. By examining how vitamin C influences immune signaling molecules called cytokines, researchers found that the supplement may influence inflammation-related processes involved in abnormal blood cell growth—suggesting a potential mechanism for its protective effect.

While the survival benefit must be confirmed in a larger phase 3 trial, the results offer genuine hope for cancer interception: intervening before cancer becomes established. Dr. Peter Jones, co-leader of the research team, emphasized that if verified, vitamin C could become "a simple way to improve care and outcomes" for vulnerable patients. For millions taking precancerous blood disorders diagnosis, this research opens a door to prevention that was previously closed.
quick_facts: 109 patients with precancerous blood disorders tested in EVITA trial
1,000 mg oral vitamin C daily for 12 months showed survival advantage
Study conducted at hospitals in Copenhagen and Los Angeles
First randomized trial of oral vitamin C for precancerous blood conditions
Participants receiving vitamin C had fewer adverse events during follow-up
